The plan

Six stops. One big idea.

Push something and it speeds up. Twist something and it spins up. That's the whole unit.

5.1

Rotational Kinematics

Describing a spin: how far around, how fast, how quickly that changes.

5.2

Linear ↔ Rotational

One spinning wheel, many speeds. The farther out you sit, the faster you fly.

5.3

Torque

A twist. It needs a force, a distance, and the right angle.

5.4

Rotational Inertia

Spinning laziness. It cares not just how much mass, but where the mass sits.

5.5

Rotational Equilibrium

Twists that cancel. Nothing changes its spin. Hello, seesaw.

5.6

Newton's 2nd Law, Spinning

Leftover twist makes a spin change. The rotating twin of \( F = ma \).

Start

Why bother

You have been doing this since you were four.

  • 1
    Doors. You push the handle, never the hinge. You already know distance from the pivot matters.
  • 2
    Seesaws. A small kid can balance a big kid by scooting back. That is torque, not muscle.
  • 3
    Wrenches. Stuck bolt? Get a longer handle. Same arm strength, way more twist.
  • 4
    Spinning in a chair. Arms out, you slow down. Arms in, you speed up. Mass placement is everything.
  • 5
    Bike gears. A small gear turning fast can drive a big wheel. Different radius, different speed.

The shortcut

Rotation looks scary because of the new Greek letters. It isn't. There are only three new quantities, and each one is the twin of something you already know.

Learn the translation table on the next slide and half of this unit is already done.

Start

The dictionary

Straight-line physics, translated.

Every rule you learned in Unit 1 has a spinning twin. Same shape of equation — just swap the letters. \\( \\Delta\\theta \\) is how far around it turned — the twin of displacement \\( \\Delta x \\), not of a parked position.

Straight lineSpinning
displacement \( \Delta x \) (m)how far it moved→angular displacement \( \Delta\theta \) (rad)how far around it turned
velocity \( v \) (m/s)→angular velocity \( \omega \) (rad/s)
acceleration \( a \) (m/s²)→angular acceleration \( \alpha \) (rad/s²)
mass \( m \) (kg)→rotational inertia \( I \) (kg·m²)
force \( F \) (N)→torque \( \tau \) (N·m)
\( v = v_0 + at \)→\( \omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t \)
\( F_{\text{net}} = ma \)→\( \tau_{\text{net}} = I\alpha \)

How to read it

The Greek letters are just nicknames:

\( \theta \) "theta" — angular displacement

\( \omega \) "omega" — spin rate

\( \alpha \) "alpha" — spin-up rate

\( \tau \) "tau" — twist

And one point sitting a distance \( r \) from the axis links the two columns:

\( s = r\theta \)  ·  \( v = r\omega \)  ·  \( a_T = r\alpha \)

If you can solve a car-speeding-up problem, you can solve a wheel-spinning-up problem. It is the same algebra with fancier handwriting.

5.1 Rotational Kinematics

Topic 5.1 · new unit of angle

Forget degrees. Meet the radian.

Take a piece of string exactly as long as the radius. Bend it around the edge of the circle. The angle it covers is one radian.

That's it. A radian is "one radius worth of curve." No 360, no protractor — the circle defines its own unit.

1 rad ≈ 57.3° π rad = half turn = 180° 2π rad = full turn ≈ 6.28

Every rotation formula in this unit assumes radians. Type 30 into a formula that wanted 0.52 and your answer is wrong by 57×. Convert first, always.

5.1 Rotational Kinematics

Topic 5.1 · how fast it spins

Angular velocity: angle eaten per second.

A record player spins at a steady rate. Every second it chews through the same number of radians. That rate is \( \omega \).

Notice what \( \omega \) is not: it is not miles per hour. It says nothing about how big the wheel is. A truck tire and a bottle cap can both spin at 5 rad/s.

+ counterclockwise − clockwise units rad/s

Pick which way is positive before you start, and write it down. Then a negative answer means "the other way," not "I made a mistake."

\[ \omega_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t} \]

how much angle ÷ how long it took

Quick one

A wheel turns 3 full circles in 2 seconds. How fast is that in rad/s?

\( \Delta\theta = 3 \times 2\pi = 18.8\,\mathrm{rad} \)

\( \omega = 18.8 / 2 = 9.4\,\mathrm{rad/s} \)

5.1 Rotational Kinematics

Topic 5.1 · spinning up

Angular acceleration: the spin rate changing.

Kick a merry-go-round and it doesn't jump to full speed. It winds up. \( \alpha \) measures how quickly \( \omega \) climbs — or falls.

If \( \alpha = 0 \), the spin is steady. Steady does not mean stopped. A ceiling fan on high has \( \omega \) large and \( \alpha \) exactly zero.

The sign trap everyone falls for

Negative \( \alpha \) does not automatically mean slowing down. It means "the twist points clockwise." Whether that speeds you up or slows you down depends on which way you were already going.

Same signs (\( \omega \) and \( \alpha \) agree) → speeding up. Opposite signs → slowing down.

\[ \alpha_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta\omega}{\Delta t} \]

change in spin rate ÷ time

Quick one

A drill goes from rest to 40 rad/s in 5 s.

\( \alpha = (40 - 0)/5 = 8\,\mathrm{rad/s^2} \)

Every second, it gains 8 rad/s of spin.

5.1 Rotational Kinematics

Topic 5.1 · the toolbox

Three equations. Pick by what's missing.

These only work when \( \alpha \) is constant. Check that first. Then look at your list of knowns and choose the equation that leaves out the thing you don't have.

No angle needed

\[ \omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t \]

straight-line twin \( v = v_0 + at \)

Use when you know the time and want the new spin rate.

No final \( \omega \) needed

\[ \theta = \theta_0 + \omega_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2}\alpha t^2 \]

straight-line twin \( x = x_0 + v_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2}a t^2 \)

Use when you want how far around it went in a given time.

No time needed

\[ \omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha(\theta - \theta_0) \]

straight-line twin \( v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a(x - x_0) \)

Use when the problem never mentions seconds — just angles and rates.

Answers come out in radians. To report revolutions, divide by \( 2\pi \). 45 rad sounds huge; it's only about 7 turns.

5.1 Rotational Kinematics

Topic 5.1 · graphs

Slope goes down the list. Area goes back up.

Same trick as straight-line graphs. Tap a graph to see what its slope and its area tell you.

Slope tells you

the angular velocity \( \omega \)

Area under it tells you

nothing useful here

Read it out loud

A straight, rising θ–t line means the wheel turns the same amount every second: steady spin.

5.1 Rotational Kinematics

Worked examples

One equation each. Watch the choosing.

A · How far around?

A wheel starts at rest and spins up at \( 2.5\,\mathrm{rad/s^2} \) for 6 s. How many turns?

No final \( \omega \) asked → use the \( \theta \) equation.

\( \theta = 0 + 0 + \tfrac12(2.5)(6)^2 \)

\( \theta = 45\,\mathrm{rad} \)

\( 45 / 2\pi \approx 7.2 \text{ turns} \)

B · How hard was the brake?

A flywheel at \( 25\,\mathrm{rad/s} \) stops after turning 125 rad. Find \( \alpha \).

No time given → use the no-\( t \) equation.

\( 0 = 25^2 + 2\alpha(125) \)

\( 250\alpha = -625 \)

\( \alpha = -2.5\,\mathrm{rad/s^2} \)

Negative because the twist fights the spin.

C · How fast at the end?

A disk already at \( 4\,\mathrm{rad/s} \) gains \( 3\,\mathrm{rad/s^2} \) for 5 s.

Time known, angle not asked → use \( \omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t \).

\( \omega = 4 + (3)(5) \)

\( \omega = 19\,\mathrm{rad/s} \)

Both positive, so it really is speeding up.

5.1 Rotational Kinematics

Practice · 5.1

Your turn. Tap to unfold the algebra.

Try each one on paper first, then open the card and compare.

Remember \( \omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t \) \( \theta = \omega_0 t + \tfrac12 \alpha t^2 \) 1 turn \( = 2\pi \) rad
1A fan blade turns through 12.6 rad in 2.0 s at a steady rate. What is \( \omega \), and how many turns is that?show the algebra
Steady rate, so just divide:

\( \omega = \Delta\theta/\Delta t = 12.6/2.0 \)

\( \omega = 6.3\,\mathrm{rad/s} \)

Turns means divide by \( 2\pi \):

\( 12.6 / 6.28 = 2.0 \text{ turns} \)

12.6 rad sounds like a lot. It's two spins.
2A merry-go-round at rest gets pushed with \( \alpha = 0.40\,\mathrm{rad/s^2} \). What is \( \omega \) after 5.0 s?show the algebra
Starts at rest, so \( \omega_0 = 0 \):

\( \omega = 0 + (0.40)(5.0) \)

\( \omega = 2.0\,\mathrm{rad/s} \)

Each second adds 0.40 rad/s. Five seconds, five helpings.
3A bike wheel spinning at \( 12\,\mathrm{rad/s} \) is braked at \( -3.0\,\mathrm{rad/s^2} \). How long until it stops?show the algebra
Stopped means \( \omega = 0 \):

\( 0 = 12 + (-3.0)t \)

\( 3.0t = 12 \)

\( t = 4.0\,\mathrm{s} \)

Opposite signs, so it really is slowing. Good sign check.
4Same wheel, same brake. How many radians does it turn while stopping?show the algebra
No time needed if you use the third equation:

\( 0 = 12^2 + 2(-3.0)\theta \)

\( 6.0\theta = 144 \)

\( \theta = 24\,\mathrm{rad} \approx 3.8 \text{ turns} \)

You could also plug \( t = 4 \) into the \( \theta \) equation. Same answer — nice check.

5.1 Rotational Kinematics

Practice · 5.1

Now the tricky ones.

These are the versions that show up on the exam. Signs and units do the damage.

Watch for degrees → radians first same signs = speeding up all points share \( \omega \)
5A turntable spins clockwise at \( 4.0\,\mathrm{rad/s} \) and has \( \alpha = +1.0\,\mathrm{rad/s^2} \) (counterclockwise). Is it speeding up or slowing down?show the reasoning
Clockwise is the negative direction, so:

\( \omega_0 = -4.0, \quad \alpha = +1.0 \)

Signs disagree → the twist fights the spin.

Slowing down — it stops at \( t = 4.0\,\mathrm{s} \), then spins the other way.

"Negative \( \alpha \) = slowing" is a myth. Compare the two signs instead.
6A wheel turns through 270° in 1.5 s. Find \( \omega \) in rad/s.show the algebra
Convert degrees to radians first:

\( 270° \times \dfrac{\pi}{180°} = 4.71\,\mathrm{rad} \)

\( \omega = 4.71/1.5 \)

\( \omega = 3.1\,\mathrm{rad/s} \)

Skip the conversion and you'd report 180 rad/s. Nearly 60× too big.
7On an \( \omega \) vs \( t \) graph, the line runs flat at \( 5\,\mathrm{rad/s} \) for 4 s. What are \( \alpha \) and \( \Delta\theta \)?show the reasoning
Slope of \( \omega \) vs \( t \) is \( \alpha \). Flat line = zero slope:

\( \alpha = 0 \)

Area under \( \omega \) vs \( t \) is \( \Delta\theta \). It's a rectangle:

\( \Delta\theta = 5 \times 4 \)

\( \Delta\theta = 20\,\mathrm{rad} \)

Zero \( \alpha \) does not mean nothing is happening. It's spinning steadily.
8Two ants ride a spinning record — one near the hole, one near the rim. Who has the bigger \( \omega \)?show the reasoning
The record is rigid: it can't twist apart.

Neither — \( \omega \) is identical for both.

Both ants complete a circle in the same time, so they sweep angle at the same rate. The rim ant covers more distance, which is Topic 5.2's whole story.

5.1 Rotational Kinematics

Topic 5.1 · recap

Pocket this.

1
Radians, always. One turn is \( 2\pi \) rad. Convert degrees before touching a formula.
2
\( \omega \) is angle per second, \( \alpha \) is \( \omega \) per second. Both are shared by every point on a rigid spinning object.
3
The big three only work if \( \alpha \) is constant. Pick the one that skips the quantity you weren't given.
4
Signs beat vocabulary. Same signs for \( \omega \) and \( \alpha \) → speeding up. Opposite → slowing.

5.1 Rotational Kinematics

Topic 5.1 · FAQ

Questions people ask about spinning.

Why radians instead of degrees?
Because radians are built from the radius, the formula \( s = r\theta \) works with no extra conversion factor. In degrees you'd need an ugly \( \pi/180 \) in every equation.
Can \( \theta \) be bigger than \( 2\pi \)?
Yes. \( \theta \) counts total angle turned, not "where the dot ended up." Ten spins is about 62.8 rad, and that's a perfectly good answer.
Is \( \omega \) the same as rpm?
Same idea, different units. rpm counts revolutions per minute; \( \omega \) counts radians per second. Convert with \( 1 \text{ rev} = 2\pi \) rad and 1 min = 60 s.
Does a bigger wheel have a bigger \( \omega \)?
No. Size never enters \( \omega \). A giant Ferris wheel can have a tiny \( \omega \) while a fidget spinner has a huge one.
What if \( \alpha \) keeps changing?
Then the big three are off-limits. You'd have to read a graph (slopes and areas still work) instead of plugging into a formula.
How do I know which equation to use?
List what you know and what you want. One of the three leaves out exactly the quantity you neither know nor need. Use that one.

5.2 Connecting Linear and Rotational Motion

Topic 5.2

Same spin. Very different speeds.

Picture a line of dancers doing a pinwheel turn, all holding hands, swinging around the dancer at one end. They all finish the turn together — same rate. But the dancer at the pivot just spins on the spot, while the dancer at the far end has to sprint to keep the line straight.

A spinning object works exactly like that. Every point shares one \( \omega \) and one \( \alpha \). What changes from point to point is \( r \) — the distance out from the axis — and that is what decides the actual speed in meters per second.

The bridge word is \( r \). Angular quantities describe the whole object. Multiply by \( r \) and you get the linear story for one specific point.

5.2 Connecting Linear and Rotational Motion

Topic 5.2 · the bridges

Three equations, one pattern: multiply by \( r \).

Look at the shape of these. It's the same sentence three times: linear = r × angular.

Distance

\[ \Delta s = r\,\Delta\theta \]

straight-line twin \( \Delta x \) — distance straight off a ruler

How far a point actually travels along its curved path. Meters, not radians.

Speed

\[ v = r\omega \]

straight-line twin \( v = \Delta x/\Delta t \)

Tangential speed — how fast that point is moving, pointing along the circle, not at the center.

Speeding up

\[ a_T = r\alpha \]

straight-line twin \( a = \Delta v/\Delta t \)

Tangential acceleration — how fast that point's speed is changing.

r is measured from the axis, not the diameter θ must be in radians double r → double v (same ω)

The three gray dots are fixed seats. The orange rider is yours.

5.2 Connecting Linear and Rotational Motion

Topic 5.2 · the sneaky part

A point on a wheel has two accelerations.

This is the single most-missed idea in 5.2. \( a_T = r\alpha \) is not the whole acceleration.

Tangential — along the path

\( a_T = r\alpha \). This one changes your speed. If the wheel spins at a steady rate, \( \alpha = 0 \) and this is zero.

Centripetal — toward the axis

\( a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{r} = r\omega^2 \). This one changes your direction. It never goes away while you're going in a circle — even at perfectly steady spin.

"The fan is at constant speed, so acceleration is zero." False. Steady circular motion still has centripetal acceleration, because the direction of motion is changing every instant.

5.2 Connecting Linear and Rotational Motion

Topic 5.2 · rolling

Rolling without slipping: spin and travel are locked together.

A wheel that grips the ground can't cheat. One full turn moves it forward by exactly one circumference — no more, no less.

That grip gives you a free equation linking the wheel's spin to how fast the whole thing travels:

\[ v_{\text{cm}} = r\omega \qquad a_{\text{cm}} = r\alpha \]

cm = center of mass. For a wheel that's the axle at its middle. So \( v_{\text{cm}} \) is how fast the bike is traveling down the road — not how fast a point on the tread is moving.

A spinning tire on ice is slipping, so this equation does not apply there. The words "rolling without slipping" are your permission slip to use it.

The weird fact

The bottom of a rolling wheel — the exact point touching the road — is momentarily at rest. Its forward motion and its backward spin cancel perfectly. That's why tire tread doesn't smear.

Try the numbers

A 0.35 m bike wheel spins at 20 rad/s.

\( v = (0.35)(20) = 7\,\mathrm{m/s} \)

That's about 25 km/h — a realistic cruising speed. Sanity checks like this catch unit mistakes.

5.2 Connecting Linear and Rotational Motion

Worked examples

Find \( r \) first. Then multiply.

A · Bicycle wheel

A wheel of radius 0.30 m spins at \( 5\,\mathrm{rad/s} \). How fast is a point on the rim moving?

\( v = r\omega = (0.30)(5) \)

\( v = 1.5\,\mathrm{m/s} \)

Radians "disappear" because they aren't a real unit — rad × m gives m.

B · Point on a CD

A mark 6.0 cm from the center rotates through \( \pi/3 \) rad. How far did it travel?

\( \Delta s = r\Delta\theta = (6.0)(1.047) \)

\( \Delta s = 6.3\,\mathrm{cm} \)

Curved distance, not a straight line across.

C · Ceiling fan, two points

Steady \( \omega = 10\,\mathrm{rad/s} \). Compare \( r = 0.20\,\mathrm{m} \) with the tip at \( r = 0.50\,\mathrm{m} \).

\( v = (0.20)(10) = 2.0\,\mathrm{m/s} \)

\( v = (0.50)(10) = 5.0\,\mathrm{m/s} \)

2.5× the radius, 2.5× the speed. Identical \( \omega \).

5.2 Connecting Linear and Rotational Motion

Practice · 5.2

Cross the bridge both ways.

Sometimes you go angular → linear, sometimes backwards. Same equation.

Remember \( v = r\omega \) \( \Delta s = r\Delta\theta \) \( a_T = r\alpha \)
1A 0.25 m radius pottery wheel spins at \( 8.0\,\mathrm{rad/s} \). How fast is the clay at the edge moving?show the algebra
Straight substitution:

\( v = (0.25)(8.0) \)

\( v = 2.0\,\mathrm{m/s} \)

Clay at half that radius would move at 1.0 m/s.
2A car tire of radius 0.32 m rolls without slipping at \( 20\,\mathrm{m/s} \). Find \( \omega \).show the algebra
Rearrange \( v = r\omega \):

\( \omega = v/r = 20/0.32 \)

\( \omega = 62.5\,\mathrm{rad/s} \)

About 10 turns every second. Sounds right for highway speed.
3A wheel of radius 0.40 m has \( \alpha = 2.0\,\mathrm{rad/s^2} \). Find \( a_T \) at the rim.show the algebra
Tangential acceleration:

\( a_T = r\alpha = (0.40)(2.0) \)

\( a_T = 0.80\,\mathrm{m/s^2} \)

That is only the speed-changing part. There's centripetal acceleration too.
4A point 10 cm from the center turns through 90°. How far does it travel along the rim?show the algebra
Convert to radians first:

\( 90° = \pi/2 = 1.571\,\mathrm{rad} \)

\( \Delta s = (10)(1.571) \)

\( \Delta s = 15.7\,\mathrm{cm} \)

Longer than the 10 cm radius, which makes sense — a quarter-circle bulges out.

5.2 Connecting Linear and Rotational Motion

Practice · 5.2

Comparison questions — the exam's favourite.

These ask "what happens if…" instead of "what number." Argue from the equation.

Watch for shared \( \omega \), different \( r \) \( a_T \) is not the only acceleration "rolling" unlocks \( v = r\omega \)
5Point A sits twice as far from the axis as point B on the same rigid disc. Compare their \( \omega \) and their \( v \).show the reasoning
Rigid body → one shared angular velocity:

\( \omega_A = \omega_B \)

From \( v = r\omega \) with \( \omega \) held constant:

\( v_A = 2v_B \)

Name the equation, say what's constant, then state the response. That's the full-credit recipe.
6A fan spins at a perfectly steady rate. A student says a blade tip has zero acceleration. Right or wrong?show the reasoning
Steady spin means \( \alpha = 0 \), so:

\( a_T = r\alpha = 0 \)

But direction is still changing, so:

Wrong — \( a_c = r\omega^2 \) is not zero. The tip accelerates toward the axis.

Constant speed is not constant velocity when you're going in a circle.
7Two gears are chained together. The small one (r = 0.05 m) spins at 20 rad/s. The chain speed is shared. Find \( \omega \) of the big gear (r = 0.15 m).show the algebra
The chain has one speed, so \( v \) matches at both rims:

\( v = (0.05)(20) = 1.0\,\mathrm{m/s} \)

Same \( v \), bigger \( r \):

\( \omega = v/r = 1.0/0.15 \)

\( \omega = 6.7\,\mathrm{rad/s} \)

Chained gears share \( v \), not \( \omega \). Points on one solid disc share \( \omega \), not \( v \). Know which situation you're in.
8A 0.30 m wheel rolls without slipping and turns through exactly 5 full revolutions. How far did the axle travel?show the algebra
Turn revolutions into radians:

\( \Delta\theta = 5(2\pi) = 31.4\,\mathrm{rad} \)

Rolling without slipping, so distance \( = r\Delta\theta \):

\( \Delta s = (0.30)(31.4) \)

\( \Delta s = 9.4\,\mathrm{m} \)

Same as 5 circumferences: \( 5 \times 2\pi(0.30) \). The grip is what makes those equal.

Topic 5.2 · recap

Pocket this.

1
\( r \) is the bridge. \( \Delta s = r\Delta\theta \), \( v = r\omega \), \( a_T = r\alpha \). Multiply an angular quantity by \( r \) to get a linear one.
2
One \( \omega \), many \( v \)'s. On a rigid object every point shares \( \omega \) and \( \alpha \); only \( r \) differs.
3
Two accelerations. \( a_T \) changes speed; \( a_c = r\omega^2 \) changes direction and survives even at steady spin.
4
Rolling without slipping locks \( v_{\text{cm}} = r\omega \). Skidding breaks the lock.

5.2 Connecting Linear and Rotational Motion

Topic 5.2 · FAQ

Questions people ask about \( v = r\omega \).

Is \( r \) the radius or the diameter?
The distance from the axis to the point you care about. If a problem hands you a 0.60 m diameter, \( r = 0.30 \) m. Halving it is the most common silent error in this topic.
Why must \( \theta \) be in radians here?
Because radians were defined so that arc length equals \( r\theta \) exactly. Degrees would need a conversion factor stapled on, and the formula would stop being clean.
Does a bigger radius mean a bigger \( \omega \)?
No — that's backwards. Radius affects the linear speed \( v \), never the angular speed. \( \omega \) belongs to the whole object.
Which way does \( v \) point?
Tangent to the circle — along the direction of travel, at a right angle to \( r \). Not outward, not inward.
When does \( v = r\omega \) fail?
When the wheel slips. A tire spinning on ice has plenty of \( \omega \) and almost no \( v \). Look for the phrase "without slipping" before using it on rolling problems.
Chained gears or one solid disc?
Points on one solid object share \( \omega \). Objects linked by a belt or chain share the rim speed \( v \). Deciding which one applies is half the problem.

5.3 Torque

Topic 5.3

Torque is a twist, not a push.

Walk up to a heavy door and shove it right next to the hinge. Push as hard as you like — it barely moves. Now push the handle with one finger. It swings.

Same force, wildly different results. Force alone doesn't decide whether something rotates. What matters is the twist — how much turning effect the force delivers about the axis.

Three ingredients make a twist: how hard you push (\( F \)), how far out you push (\( r \)), and the angle you push at (\( \theta \)). Weaken any one of them and the twist shrinks.

units N·m + counterclockwise − clockwise

5.3 Torque

Topic 5.3 · the equation

Three ingredients, multiplied.

\[ \tau = rF\sin\theta = rF_\perp \]

twist = distance × force × how square-on you push

\( r \) — distance from the axis to where the force lands, in meters.
\( F \) — how hard you push, in newtons.
\( \theta \) — the angle between the force arrow and the line \( r \). Not the angle to the floor.
\( F_\perp \) — the slice of the force that is square-on to \( r \). That slice is the only part that twists.

The sine, in plain words

\( \sin 90° = 1 \) → push square-on, you get every bit of twist: \( \tau = rF \).

\( \sin 30° = 0.5 \) → push at a slant, half wasted.

\( \sin 0° = 0 \) → push straight along the handle, nothing happens.

On the AP exam you only ever calculate the size of a torque plus its sense (clockwise or counterclockwise). Full 3-D torque direction is off the syllabus. One less thing to memorize.

5.3 Torque

Lab 4 · try it

Loosen the bolt. Find the sweet spot.

Drag the three sliders. The dashed gray line is the force's line of action; the blue bracket is the lever arm. Watch what the angle does to your twist.

Pull square-on (90°) for the maximum possible twist.

Torque \( \tau \)
15.0 N·m
Lever arm
0.30 m
\( F_\perp \)
50.0 N
Best possible
15.0 N·m

τ = (0.30)(50)(sin 90°) = 15.0 N·m

100% of the best you could do at this r and F

5.3 Torque

Topic 5.3 · lever arm

The lever arm is a shortcut for the same idea.

Extend the force arrow into an infinite straight line — that's its line of action. Now measure the shortest distance from the axis to that line. That distance is the lever arm.

\[ \text{lever arm} = r\sin\theta \qquad \tau = F \times (\text{lever arm}) \]

Two ways to slice the same product. Either trim the force down to \( F_\perp \), or trim the distance down to the lever arm. Never trim both — you'd be applying the \( \sin\theta \) twice.

Why this explains your life

Long wrench handles. Bigger \( r \) means a bigger lever arm, so a normal human can beat a rusted bolt.

Door handles far from hinges. Designers hand you the longest lever arm the door allows.

Bottle openers, nutcrackers, scissors. All the same trick: trade distance for force.

A small force with a long lever arm can beat a huge force with a short one. This is why "bigger force means bigger torque" is a trap.

5.3 Torque

Topic 5.3 · the zeros

Two ways to push hard and achieve nothing.

Zero #1

Push straight at the axis

If your force points directly toward or away from the pivot, \( \theta = 0° \) or \( 180° \), so \( \sin\theta = 0 \) and \( \tau = 0 \).

You're trying to squash the object into the axle instead of spinning it. Think of pushing a merry-go-round bar toward the center pole.

Zero #2

Push right at the pivot

If the force lands on the axis itself, \( r = 0 \), so \( \tau = 0 \) no matter how enormous the force is.

This is secretly useful: in Topic 5.5 you'll deliberately put your pivot on an unknown force so it drops out of the equation.

\( \theta = 90° \)

\( \sin\theta = 1 \) → full twist, \( \tau = rF \)

\( \theta = 30° \)

\( \sin\theta = 0.5 \) → half the twist

\( \theta = 0° \) or \( 180° \)

\( \sin\theta = 0 \) → no twist at all

5.3 Torque

Topic 5.3 · drawing it

For rotation, where the force lands is part of the answer.

A normal free-body diagram bunches every arrow at the center of mass. That's fine for \( F = ma \) — and useless for torque.

So rotation problems use a force diagram instead: same arrows, but each one is drawn at the exact spot where it acts, with the axis clearly marked.

  • 1
    Mark the axis or pivot first.
  • 2
    Draw each force at its real point of application.
  • 3
    Label each \( r \) from the axis.
  • 4
    Note the angle between each force and its \( r \).

5.3 Torque

Worked examples

Three twists, three angles.

A · Door push

You push a door with 15 N, square-on, 0.75 m from the hinge.

\( \tau = (0.75)(15)\sin 90° \)

\( \tau = 11.25\,\mathrm{N{\cdot}m} \)

Square-on, so the sine is just 1 and disappears.

B · Wrench at a slant

50 N at 0.30 m, but pulled at only 30° to the handle.

\( \tau = (0.30)(50)(0.5) = 7.5 \)

Now straighten your wrist to 90°:

\( \tau_{\max} = (0.30)(50) = 15 \)

Same arm strength, double the twist. Free upgrade.

C · Rod at 60°

20 N applied 0.40 m from the pivot, at 60° to the rod.

\( \sin 60° = 0.866 \)

\( \tau = (0.40)(20)(0.866) \)

\( \tau = 6.93\,\mathrm{N{\cdot}m} \)

Drop the sine and you'd claim 8.0 — about 15% too generous.

5.3 Torque

Practice · 5.3

Twist it yourself.

Torque is the most-missed topic in this unit. These four are the reason why.

Remember \( \tau = rF\sin\theta \) \( \theta \) is between \( F \) and \( r \) lever arm \( = r\sin\theta \)
1A 25 N force is applied square-on, 0.40 m from a pivot. Find the torque.show the algebra
Square-on means \( \theta = 90° \), \( \sin 90° = 1 \):

\( \tau = (0.40)(25)(1) \)

\( \tau = 10\,\mathrm{N{\cdot}m} \)

Newton-meters, not newtons. Torque and force have different units.
2Same 25 N and 0.40 m, but now at 30° to the rod. Find the torque and the lever arm.show the algebra
Apply the sine:

\( \tau = (0.40)(25)(0.5) \)

\( \tau = 5.0\,\mathrm{N{\cdot}m} \)

Lever arm is the trimmed distance:

\( r\sin\theta = (0.40)(0.5) = 0.20\,\mathrm{m} \)

Half the angle-effectiveness, half the torque. And \( (25)(0.20) = 5.0 \) — the two methods agree.
3A student pushes a merry-go-round bar straight toward the center pole with 200 N. What torque does it produce?show the reasoning
Force points along \( r \), so \( \theta = 0° \):

\( \sin 0° = 0 \)

\( \tau = 0 \) — no spin at all

All 200 N goes into squeezing the axle. Huge force, zero twist.
4You need 24 N·m to crack a bolt but can only pull 60 N square-on. How long a wrench do you need?show the algebra
Solve \( \tau = rF \) for \( r \):

\( r = \tau/F = 24/60 \)

\( r = 0.40\,\mathrm{m} \)

Can't push harder? Reach farther. That's the whole engineering trick.

5.3 Torque

Practice · 5.3

Compare, don't just compute.

The exam loves "how does \( \tau \) change if…". Answer from the equation, not from a calculator.

Watch for bigger F ≠ bigger τ never double-count \( \sin\theta \) angle from \( r \), not the ground
5Ana pushes 40 N at 0.20 m from the hinge. Ben pushes 20 N at 0.50 m. Both square-on. Who wins?show the reasoning
Compute both twists:

\( \tau_{\text{Ana}} = (0.20)(40) = 8.0 \)

\( \tau_{\text{Ben}} = (0.50)(20) = 10.0 \)

Ben — even though Ana pushes twice as hard.

The lever arm won. This is exactly why "more force = more torque" fails.
6A force is applied at 30°. You rotate your wrist to 90° with everything else unchanged. What happens to \( \tau \)?show the reasoning
Only \( \sin\theta \) changes:

\( \sin 30° = 0.5 \rightarrow \sin 90° = 1.0 \)

The torque doubles.

Functional reasoning: name the factor, state how it changes, state the effect. No numbers needed.
7Two forces act on a rod pivoted at its center: 12 N down at 0.5 m left, and 12 N down at 0.5 m right. Find the net torque.show the reasoning
Left side pushed down → turns counterclockwise (+):

\( \tau_1 = +(0.5)(12) = +6.0 \)

Right side pushed down → turns clockwise (−):

\( \tau_2 = -(0.5)(12) = -6.0 \)

\( \tau_{\text{net}} = 0 \)

Two real torques that cancel. Straight into Topic 5.5.
8A 30 N force at 0.60 m gives a lever arm of 0.30 m. What angle was it applied at?show the algebra
Lever arm \( = r\sin\theta \):

\( 0.30 = 0.60\sin\theta \)

\( \sin\theta = 0.5 \)

\( \theta = 30° \) (or 150° — same sine)

Two angles share a sine. Both give the same size of twist.

5.3 Torque

Topic 5.3 · recap

Pocket this.

1
\( \tau = rF\sin\theta = rF_\perp \). Units N·m. Only the square-on slice of the force twists anything.
2
\( \theta \) is measured between \( F \) and \( r \) — never between \( F \) and the ground. Sketch both arrows from the same point before you decide.
3
Lever arm \( = r\sin\theta \). Either shrink the force or shrink the distance. Not both.
4
Two zeros: pushing at the axis (\( r = 0 \)) and pushing along \( r \) (\( \sin\theta = 0 \)).

5.3 Torque

Topic 5.3 · FAQ

Questions people ask about torque.

Is torque just another word for force?
No. Force is a push; torque is a twist that a push produces about a chosen axis. Same force can give a huge torque, a small one, or zero, depending on where and how it's applied.
Which angle is \( \theta \)?
The angle between the force arrow and the position vector \( r \) drawn from the axis to the force's point of application. Draw both arrows starting at the same spot and the angle is obvious.
Do I use \( \sin \) or \( \cos \)?
\( \sin \), as long as \( \theta \) is measured from \( r \). If a problem hands you the angle from the perpendicular instead, that's the complement and \( \cos \) would apply — which is why sketching first beats memorizing.
Can torque be negative?
Yes, and it should be. Pick counterclockwise as positive and clockwise torques come out negative. Those signs are what let torques cancel in equilibrium problems.
Does the axis have to be a real axle?
No. You can compute torque about any point you like — even an imaginary one. Torque values change with your choice of axis, which is a feature, not a bug (see 5.5).
Do I need the 3-D direction of torque?
Not in AP Physics 1. Magnitude plus clockwise/counterclockwise is all that's assessed. Skip the right-hand rule for now.

5.4 Rotational Inertia

Topic 5.4

Mass that cares where it sits.

Hold a broom by the handle end and swing it. Now grab it in the middle and swing it. Same broom, same mass — but the second one is dramatically easier.

Nothing about the amount of stuff changed. What changed is how far that stuff sits from the axis you're spinning around. That's rotational inertia, \( I \).

Symbol \( I \) — capital i, not a one
Units kg·m²
Role the twin of mass \( m \)

Mass tells you how hard something is to get moving in a straight line. Rotational inertia tells you how hard it is to get spinning — and it depends on your choice of axis.

5.4 Rotational Inertia

Topic 5.4 · the equation

One little mass: \( I = mr^2 \).

\[ I = mr^2 \qquad I_{\text{total}} = \sum m_i r_i^2 \]

add up every mass times its distance squared

That square is the whole story

Move a mass twice as far from the axis and it contributes four times as much. Three times as far → nine times as much.

So the outer parts of an object dominate. A hollow hoop is much harder to spin than a solid disc of the same mass, because all the hoop's mass sits at the maximum radius.

If the axis goes through the mass

Then \( r = 0 \), so \( mr^2 = 0 \). That mass contributes nothing. Free points on the exam — just notice it.

You'll only ever hand-calculate \( I \) for about five point masses. For real shapes — discs, rods, spheres — the exam hands you the formula. Your job is to explain why one is bigger than another.

5.4 Rotational Inertia

Lab 5 · try it

Slide the weights and watch \( I \) explode.

Two blocks on a light rod. Change their masses and their distances from the axis. Because of the square, distance is far more powerful than mass.

Try this: set both masses to 2 kg. Put one at 0.4 m and the other at 0.8 m. The far one contributes 4× as much.

\( m_1r_1^2 \)
0.48
\( m_2r_2^2 \)
0.98
Total \( I \)
1.46

I = (3.0)(0.40)² + (2.0)(0.70)² = 1.46 kg·m²

the lighter mass is doing more of the work

5.4 Rotational Inertia

Lab 6 · try it

Race three shapes down a ramp.

A hoop, a solid disc, and a solid ball — all released together. Guess the winner before you press Race. Then try changing the mass and the radius.

on your marks
Shape\( I \)a (m/s²)t (s)
Ball0.4MR²——
Disc0.5MR²——
Hoop1.0MR²——

Ball first, then disc, then hoop — every single time.

Why

All the hoop's mass sits out at the rim, where \( r^2 \) is biggest. That makes it the laziest spinner, so more of gravity's help goes into spinning it up instead of moving it forward.

5.4 Rotational Inertia

Topic 5.4 · moving the axis

Move the axle away from the center, and \( I \) always grows.

The center of mass is the easiest place to spin about. Slide your axis anywhere else — staying parallel — and spinning gets harder by a predictable amount.

\[ I' = I_{\text{cm}} + Md^2 \]

\( d \) = how far you shifted the axis

Notice \( Md^2 \) is never negative. Any shift makes \( I \) bigger. There is no clever axis that beats the center of mass.

This only works from a center-of-mass axis to a parallel one. You can't hop between two random axes with it.

Worked · shifting a rod

A 4 kg rod has \( I_{\text{cm}} = 0.80\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2} \). Move the axis 0.20 m off center.

\( I' = 0.80 + (4)(0.20)^2 \)

\( I' = 0.80 + 0.16 = 0.96 \)

Worked · disc to the rim

A 5 kg disc, \( R = 0.30 \) m, has \( I_{\text{cm}} = 0.225 \). Now spin it about a point on its edge.

\( I' = 0.225 + 5(0.30)^2 \)

\( I' = 0.225 + 0.45 = 0.675 \)

Three times harder to spin, same disc.

5.4 Rotational Inertia

Lab 7 · try it

Slide the axis along a two-mass rod.

Same two masses, same rod. Only the axis moves — and \( I \) changes the whole time.

Drag the axis and watch which mass is doing the damage.

The dashed marker is the center of mass. Nowhere beats it — slide the axis either way and \( I \) only climbs. That is the parallel axis theorem, felt rather than derived.

\( r_1 \) to 3 kg
0.40 m
\( r_2 \) to 2 kg
0.70 m
\( I \) about this axis
1.46 kg·m²

I = 3(0.40)² + 2(0.70)² = 1.46

Park the axis on a mass and it contributes nothing — but the other one is now a full 1.10 m out, and distance is squared.

5.4 Rotational Inertia

Worked examples

Find the axis. Measure each \( r \). Square. Add.

A · Two masses on a rod

3 kg at 0.40 m and 2 kg at 0.70 m from the axis. Rod's own mass is ignorable.

\( I = (3)(0.40)^2 + (2)(0.70)^2 \)

\( I = 0.48 + 0.98 \)

\( I = 1.46\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2} \)

The lighter mass contributes more, because it sits farther out.

B · Now move the axis

Same two masses, but put the axis right on the 3 kg block. The 2 kg block is now 1.10 m away.

\( I = (3)(0)^2 + (2)(1.10)^2 \)

\( I = 0 + 2.42 \)

\( I = 2.42\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2} \)

Bigger than before — and a whole 3 kg dropped out for free.

C · Hoop vs disc

Both 2 kg, both \( R = 0.5 \) m, both spun about the center.

hoop: \( I = MR^2 = 0.50 \)

disc: \( I = \tfrac12MR^2 = 0.25 \)

Identical mass, identical size, double the rotational inertia. Placement wins.

5.4 Rotational Inertia

Practice · 5.4

Square the distance. Every time.

Forgetting to square \( r \) is the single most expensive mistake in this topic.

Remember \( I = \sum m_ir_i^2 \) \( I' = I_{\text{cm}} + Md^2 \) units kg·m²
1A 0.5 kg ball is whirled on a 2.0 m string. Find \( I \) about the hand.show the algebra
Single point mass:

\( I = mr^2 = (0.5)(2.0)^2 \)

\( I = 2.0\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2} \)

Only 0.5 kg, but 2 m out. The square does the heavy lifting.
2Two 1.5 kg masses sit at 0.30 m on opposite sides of a central axis. Find the total \( I \).show the algebra
Distance is a distance — opposite sides still count as +0.30:

\( I = (1.5)(0.30)^2 + (1.5)(0.30)^2 \)

\( I = 0.135 + 0.135 \)

\( I = 0.27\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2} \)

There are no negative \( r \)'s in \( I \). Squaring erases the sign anyway.
3A mass sits 0.20 m from the axis. You slide it out to 0.60 m. By what factor does its \( I \) change?show the reasoning
The distance tripled, and \( I \propto r^2 \):

\( 3^2 = 9 \)

9 times bigger

You didn't add a gram of mass. Sliding it out was enough.
4A 3.0 kg disc has \( I_{\text{cm}} = 0.15\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2} \). Find \( I \) about a parallel axis 0.25 m away.show the algebra
Parallel axis theorem:

\( I' = 0.15 + (3.0)(0.25)^2 \)

\( I' = 0.15 + 0.1875 \)

\( I' \approx 0.34\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2} \)

Adding, never subtracting. Off-center is always harder.
5A light aluminium hoop and a heavy solid steel ball are the same size. Can the lighter hoop have the bigger \( I \)?show the reasoning
Compare the shape factors:

hoop: \( I = 1.0\,MR^2 \)

ball: \( I = 0.4\,MR^2 \)

Yes — if the hoop's mass is more than 40% of the ball's.

Mass alone never settles it. Where the mass sits can outvote how much there is.
6A skater pulls her arms in mid-spin. What happens to \( I \), and why does she speed up?show the reasoning
Her arm mass moves to a smaller \( r \):

\( I \) decreases.

No outside twist acted on her, so her spin has to compensate by getting faster. (The full bookkeeping for that trade is angular momentum, in Unit 6 — here, just notice \( I \) is not a fixed property of a body.)

5.4 Rotational Inertia

Topic 5.4 · recap

Pocket this.

1
\( I = \sum m_ir_i^2 \). Rotational inertia is the \( m \) of the spinning world. Units kg·m².
2
The square is everything. Twice as far out means four times the contribution. Rim mass dominates.
3
\( I \) is not a property of an object alone — it depends on which axis you pick. Change the axis, change \( I \).
4
\( I' = I_{\text{cm}} + Md^2 \). The center of mass is always the easiest axis; any parallel shift costs you \( Md^2 \).

5.4 Rotational Inertia

Topic 5.4 · FAQ

Questions people ask about rotational inertia.

Is \( I \) the same thing as mass?
It plays the same role — resisting change — but it isn't the same quantity. Two objects of identical mass can have completely different \( I \) depending on how that mass is spread out.
What exactly is \( r \)?
The shortest, perpendicular distance from the axis to that bit of mass. Not the object's width, not the distance to its center, not whatever length is printed on the diagram.
Do I have to memorize formulas for discs and rods?
No. The AP exam supplies those. You are expected to hand-calculate only small sets of point masses — up to about five — and to explain comparisons in words.
Why does the hoop beat the disc?
Every gram of a hoop is at the maximum radius. A disc has plenty of material near the middle contributing almost nothing, because \( r^2 \) is tiny there.
Can \( I \) ever be zero?
Only if all the mass sits exactly on the axis — a genuine point mass on its own axis. Real extended objects always have some \( I \).
Does the parallel axis theorem work between any two axes?
No. One of the two must pass through the center of mass. To go between two off-center axes, travel via the center of mass in two steps.

5.5 Rotational Equilibrium

Topic 5.5

When all the twists cancel, the spin stops changing.

A balanced seesaw isn't torque-free. There are two big torques on it — they just happen to be equal and opposite, so the seesaw's spin never changes.

\[ \sum \tau_i = 0 \]

clockwise twists = counterclockwise twists

This is Newton's first law, rewritten for spinning: no net twist means no change in the spin.

Equilibrium ≠ standing still

A wheel humming along at a rock-steady 40 rad/s is in rotational equilibrium. So is a wheel sitting dead still. Both have \( \omega \) that isn't changing.

The word to underline is constant, not zero.

Signs are your friend here. Call counterclockwise positive, clockwise negative, and "they cancel" becomes ordinary algebra: the terms add to zero.

5.5 Rotational Equilibrium

Topic 5.5 · two kinds

Balanced forces and balanced twists are different jobs.

These two conditions do not come as a package. You can have either one without the other, so you have to check them separately.

Translational equilibrium

\( \sum \vec{F} = 0 \)

The center of mass moves at constant velocity — it isn't speeding up or turning as a whole.

Rotational equilibrium

\( \sum \tau = 0 \)

The spin rate \( \omega \) stays constant — it isn't spinning up or slowing down.

Both, at once

A book lying on a table. Nothing moves, nothing spins.

Rotational only

A wheel pulled forward by its axle: it accelerates across the floor, but the pull creates no torque about its own center, so its spin rate holds steady.

Translational only

A spinning top gliding across a table at steady speed while friction slowly spins it down.

Never write "it's in equilibrium" and stop. Say which equilibrium. Half the credit on these questions lives in that distinction.

5.5 Rotational Equilibrium

Lab 8 · try it

Balance it without changing anyone's weight.

Two kids, two distances. The plank tilts toward whichever side is winning. Can you balance a 45 kg kid against a 20 kg kid?

tilting left Move the lighter kid farther out.
Left twist (+)
+441
Right twist (−)
−196
Net twist
+245

net τ = (45)(9.8)(1.00) − (20)(9.8)(1.00) = +245 N·m

Balanced means \( m_1d_1 = m_2d_2 \). Gravity cancels out of both sides.

5.5 Rotational Equilibrium

Topic 5.5 · the pro move

Put your pivot on the force you don't know.

Here's a trick that feels like cheating. You get to choose where the axis goes. Anything sitting at the axis has \( r = 0 \), so its torque is zero — and it vanishes from your equation.

Hinge force you can't calculate? Put the axis on the hinge. Mystery support force? Axis goes there. One unknown, gone, without any extra algebra.

  • 1
    Pick the axis — ideally right on an unknown force.
  • 2
    Draw a force diagram showing where each force acts.
  • 3
    Write each torque as \( rF\sin\theta \).
  • 4
    Give each a + or − for its turning direction.
  • 5
    Set the sum to zero and solve.

Also handy

If an object's weight acts at the pivot — like a uniform plank balanced at its exact middle — its own weight makes zero torque. You can ignore the plank entirely.

A smart pivot is a convenience, not a rule. Any axis gives a correct equation for an object in rotational equilibrium; some just give easier equations.

5.5 Rotational Equilibrium

Worked examples

Set the sum to zero and solve.

A · Seesaw

A 25 kg child sits 1.0 m left of the pivot. Where does a 40 kg child sit to balance?

\( -(25)(9.8)(1.0) + (40)(9.8)x = 0 \)

\( 392x = 245 \)

\( x = 0.625\,\mathrm{m} \)

The heavier kid sits closer. \( g \) cancels — you never really needed it.

B · Meter stick

Balanced at the 50 cm mark. A 200 g mass hangs at 20 cm. Where does a 150 g mass go?

\( (0.200)(0.30) = (0.150)(x) \)

\( x = 0.40\,\mathrm{m} \) right of center

→ the 90 cm mark

Convert marks into distances-from-pivot before you start.

C · Hinged sign

An 80 N sign hangs at the middle of a 2.0 m light beam. A cable at the far end pulls at 30° to the beam. Find the tension.

Axis on the hinge → hinge force drops out.

\( (1.0)(80) = (2.0)T\sin 30° \)

\( 80 = 1.0\,T \)

\( T = 80\,\mathrm{N} \)

5.5 Rotational Equilibrium

Practice · 5.5

Balance these.

Every one of these is "write \( \sum\tau = 0 \), then solve for the one letter left."

Remember \( \sum\tau = 0 \) CCW +, CW − pivot on the unknown
1A 30 kg child sits 2.0 m from a seesaw's pivot. A 40 kg child sits on the other side. How far out?show the algebra
Balance the two twists (\( g \) cancels):

\( (30)(2.0) = (40)(d) \)

\( 60 = 40d \)

\( d = 1.5\,\mathrm{m} \)

Heavier kid, shorter lever arm. Always.
2A 4.0 m plank rests on a central pivot. A 100 N box sits 1.5 m left. What upward force at the right end balances it?show the algebra
The right end is 2.0 m from the pivot:

\( (1.5)(100) = (2.0)F \)

\( 150 = 2.0F \)

\( F = 75\,\mathrm{N} \)

Farther out means you need less force. That's a lever.
3A wheel is pulled forward by a rope tied to its axle and speeds up across the floor. Is it in rotational equilibrium?show the reasoning
The rope acts at the axis, so \( r = 0 \):

\( \tau_{\text{rope}} = 0 \)

Yes for rotation, no for translation.

Its center of mass accelerates while its spin rate holds constant. The two equilibria really are independent.
4A uniform 60 N beam, 3.0 m long, is held horizontal by a hinge at the left end and a vertical cable at the right end. Find the cable tension.show the algebra
Uniform beam → its weight acts at the middle, 1.5 m out. Axis on the hinge:

\( (1.5)(60) = (3.0)T \)

\( 90 = 3.0T \)

\( T = 30\,\mathrm{N} \)

The cable holds half the weight because it's twice as far out as the weight's center.
5Why can you ignore the hinge force when you take torques about the hinge?show the reasoning
Its point of application is the axis:

\( \tau = rF\sin\theta = (0)F\sin\theta \)

\( \tau_{\text{hinge}} = 0 \)

The force is still there and still real. It just produces no twist about that particular point.
6A gymnast holds a perfect handstand, perfectly still. Which equilibrium conditions hold?show the reasoning
Nothing translating and nothing spinning:

Both — \( \sum\vec{F} = 0 \) and \( \sum\tau = 0 \).

This is why holding a handstand is so hard: the gymnast is constantly making tiny finger adjustments to keep the net torque at zero.

5.5 Rotational Equilibrium

Topic 5.5 · recap

Pocket this.

1
\( \sum\tau = 0 \) means \( \omega \) is constant — which includes zero, but doesn't require it.
2
Force balance and torque balance are separate checks. Either can hold while the other fails.
3
Choose your pivot on an unknown force and it disappears from the torque equation for free.
4
Seesaw shortcut: \( m_1d_1 = m_2d_2 \). Gravity appears on both sides and cancels.

5.5 Rotational Equilibrium

Topic 5.5 · FAQ

Questions people ask about balance.

Does rotational equilibrium mean it's not spinning?
No. It means the spin rate isn't changing. A flywheel at a steady 100 rad/s qualifies just as much as one sitting still.
If forces are balanced, are torques balanced too?
Not necessarily. Two equal and opposite forces applied at different spots add to zero force but produce a real net twist. Check both conditions separately, every time.
Where should I put the pivot?
Wherever kills the most unknowns — usually right on a hinge or support whose force you weren't given. Any choice is valid; some are just less work.
Do I include the plank's own weight?
Yes, if the plank has mass. Treat it as a single force at the plank's center. If the pivot happens to be at that center, that torque is zero and you can skip it.
Why does \( g \) keep cancelling?
Because it multiplies every weight term equally. In pure balance problems you can compare \( m_1d_1 \) with \( m_2d_2 \) and never type 9.8 at all.
What if there are three or four forces?
Same method — just more terms. Give each a sign, add them up, set to zero. Choosing a pivot that zeroes one of them keeps the algebra sane.

5.5 Rotational Equilibrium

Topic 5.5 · cheatsheet

5.5 on one page.

5.6 Newton's Second Law in Rotational Form

Topic 5.6

Leftover twist makes the spin change.

In 5.5 the twists cancelled and nothing changed. Now let one side win. That leftover twist is what spins things up — and how fast it spins them up depends on how lazy the object is.

\[ \alpha = \frac{\tau_{\text{net}}}{I} \]

spin-up rate = leftover twist ÷ spinning laziness

Put it next to \( a = F_{\text{net}}/m \) and the family resemblance is unmistakable. Same law, spinning costume.

Read the fractions

Double the torque → double \( \alpha \). It's on top.

Double the inertia → half \( \alpha \). It's on the bottom.

Zero net torque → \( \alpha = 0 \), constant spin. That's 5.5 falling out as a special case.

\( \alpha \) always points the same way as \( \tau_{\text{net}} \). A counterclockwise leftover twist spins things counterclockwise-er.

5.6 Newton's Second Law in Rotational Form

Lab 9 · try it

Two dials. Watch the wheel obey.

Crank the torque and the wheel spins up faster. Crank the rotational inertia and it sulks. The gold wheel is the same wheel with half the inertia — same twist, double the spin-up.

5.6 Newton's Second Law in Rotational Form

Topic 5.6 · method

Four steps, every time.

  • 1
    Draw a force diagram. Mark the axis, and put each arrow where it really acts.
  • 2
    Torque each force. \( \tau = rF\sin\theta \), with a + or − for its direction.
  • 3
    Add them up to get \( \tau_{\text{net}} \).
  • 4
    Divide by \( I \) to get \( \alpha \). Done — unless something also moves in a straight line.

Worked · door

A 20 kg door, 1.0 m wide, has \( I = 20/3\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2} \) about its hinge. You push 15 N square-on at the far edge.

\( \tau = (1.0)(15) = 15\,\mathrm{N{\cdot}m} \)

\( \alpha = 15 \div (20/3) \)

\( \alpha = 2.25\,\mathrm{rad/s^2} \)

Do not plug a force where a torque belongs. \( \alpha = F/I \) is not a thing. Convert force to torque first.

5.6 Newton's Second Law in Rotational Form

Topic 5.6 · combined systems

When something spins and travels, you need both laws.

A block on a rope over a real pulley is two problems glued together. The block goes straight down; the pulley spins. They are connected by the rope.

\[ \sum F = ma \qquad \sum\tau = I\alpha \qquad a = r\alpha \]

two laws, plus the rope's promise

That third equation, \( a = r\alpha \), is the glue. It says the rope doesn't stretch or slip: however fast the rim moves, the block moves.

The trap: unequal tensions

If the pulley has real rotational inertia, the two rope tensions are not equal. The difference is exactly what spins the pulley up:

\( \tau_{\text{net}} = (T_2 - T_1)r = I\alpha \)

Only a massless, frictionless pulley lets you write \( T_1 = T_2 \). If the problem gives you \( I \), it's telling you the tensions differ.

Same idea for a yo-yo or a rolling can: write \( F = ma \) for the center of mass, \( \tau = I\alpha \) about the center, then bolt them together with \( a = r\alpha \).

5.6 Newton's Second Law in Rotational Form

Worked examples

From a one-liner to the full pulley.

A · Compare two discs

Same torque on two same-size discs. Disc A's \( \alpha \) is twice Disc B's. Compare their masses.

\( \alpha = \tau/I \Rightarrow I_A = \tfrac12 I_B \)

Same shape and radius means \( I \propto M \):

\( M_A = \tfrac12 M_B \)

B is twice as heavy, so it spins up half as fast.

B · Simple wheel

A 0.20 m pulley with \( I = 0.05\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2} \) is pulled by a 4.0 N rope on its rim.

\( \tau = (0.20)(4.0) = 0.80 \)

\( \alpha = 0.80/0.05 \)

\( \alpha = 16\,\mathrm{rad/s^2} \)

Rope on the rim pulls at 90° to \( r \), so no sine to worry about.

C · Pulley with two blocks

\( m_1 = 2.0 \) kg rising, \( m_2 = 3.0 \) kg falling, \( r = 0.10 \) m, \( I = 0.002\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2} \).

\( T_1 = m_1(g + a) \)

\( T_2 = m_2(g - a) \)

\( (T_2 - T_1)r = I(a/r) \)

\( 0.98 = 0.52a \Rightarrow a = 1.9\,\mathrm{m/s^2} \)

\( \alpha = a/r \approx 19\,\mathrm{rad/s^2} \)

5.6 Newton's Second Law in Rotational Form

Practice · 5.6

Twist in, spin-up out.

Get the torque right first. Then it's just a division.

Remember \( \alpha = \tau_{\text{net}}/I \) \( \tau = rF\sin\theta \) \( \alpha \) follows \( \tau_{\text{net}} \)
1A net torque of 12 N·m acts on a wheel with \( I = 3.0\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2} \). Find \( \alpha \).show the algebra
Straight division:

\( \alpha = 12/3.0 \)

\( \alpha = 4.0\,\mathrm{rad/s^2} \)

Same shape as \( a = F/m \), just with the spinning letters.
2A 6.0 N force pulls a rope wrapped around a 0.25 m pulley with \( I = 0.30\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2} \). Find \( \alpha \).show the algebra
Torque first — the rope leaves the rim at 90°:

\( \tau = (0.25)(6.0) = 1.5 \)

Then divide:

\( \alpha = 1.5/0.30 \)

\( \alpha = 5.0\,\mathrm{rad/s^2} \)

Two steps, in that order. Never divide the force by \( I \).
3The same net torque is applied to a hoop and a disc of equal mass and radius. Which gets the bigger \( \alpha \)?show the reasoning
Compare their rotational inertias:

hoop \( I = MR^2 \), disc \( I = \tfrac12MR^2 \)

\( \alpha = \tau/I \) with \( \tau \) fixed:

The disc — exactly twice the \( \alpha \) of the hoop.

Half the \( I \), double the \( \alpha \). That's the inverse relationship doing its job.
4You want to double a wheel's \( \alpha \) but can't change the force. Name two things you could do.show the reasoning
Attack the fraction from either side:

Double \( r \) (doubling \( \tau \)), or halve \( I \).

You could also fix a sloppy angle — if you were pushing at 30°, straightening to 90° doubles \( \tau \) all by itself.

5.6 Newton's Second Law in Rotational Form

Practice · 5.6

Spinning and traveling at once.

Two equations plus the glue. These are the hardest problems in the unit — take them slowly.

Watch for \( a = r\alpha \) is required \( T_1 \neq T_2 \) when \( I \neq 0 \) one equation per object
5A pulley's rim moves with \( a = 2.4\,\mathrm{m/s^2} \) and \( r = 0.12 \) m. Find \( \alpha \).show the algebra
Use the glue equation, rearranged:

\( \alpha = a/r = 2.4/0.12 \)

\( \alpha = 20\,\mathrm{rad/s^2} \)

Small pulley, big \( \alpha \). Dividing by a small radius blows the number up.
6A 1.5 kg block hangs from a rope wound around a pulley with no rotational inertia (\( I = 0 \)). Find \( a \) and the tension.show the algebra
Pulley: \( Tr = I\alpha \), and \( I = 0 \), so:

\( Tr = 0 \Rightarrow T = 0 \)

Block: \( mg - T = ma \) with \( T = 0 \):

\( a = g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2} \), \( T = 0 \)

An inertia-free pulley takes nothing for itself, so the block just free-falls. Compare it with the next problem.
7A 1.5 kg block hangs from a rope wound around a pulley with \( I = 0.09\,\mathrm{kg{\cdot}m^2} \) and \( r = 0.20 \) m. Find \( a \).show the algebra
Block: \( mg - T = ma \), so \( T = m(g-a) \). Pulley: \( Tr = I\alpha = I(a/r) \).

\( m(g-a)r = Ia/r \)

\( (1.5)(9.8-a)(0.20) = 0.09a/0.20 \)

\( 2.94 - 0.30a = 0.45a \)

\( a \approx 3.9\,\mathrm{m/s^2} \)

Same block as problem 6, but now less than half of \( g \). The pulley's laziness is holding it back.
8Two blocks hang over a pulley with real rotational inertia. A student writes \( T_1 = T_2 \). What's wrong?show the reasoning
A pulley with \( I \neq 0 \) needs a net torque to spin up:

\( (T_2 - T_1)r = I\alpha \)

If \( \alpha \neq 0 \) and \( I \neq 0 \), then \( T_2 \neq T_1 \).

Equal tensions would give zero net torque and the pulley would never start turning.

5.6 Newton's Second Law in Rotational Form

Topic 5.6 · recap

Pocket this.

1
\( \alpha = \tau_{\text{net}}/I \). The spinning twin of \( a = F_{\text{net}}/m \), and \( \alpha \) points the way \( \tau_{\text{net}} \) does.
2
Torque on top, inertia on the bottom. Double \( \tau \) → double \( \alpha \). Double \( I \) → half \( \alpha \).
3
Combined systems need both laws plus \( a = r\alpha \) to link them.
4
A real pulley has \( T_1 \neq T_2 \). That difference is what supplies its net torque.

5.6 Newton's Second Law in Rotational Form

Topic 5.6 · FAQ

Questions people ask about \( \tau = I\alpha \).

Can a force cause \( \alpha \) directly?
No — only torque does. A force applied at the axis, or pointing straight at it, produces no \( \alpha \) at all no matter how strong it is.
Does zero net torque mean it stops spinning?
No. It means the spin rate stops changing. Whatever \( \omega \) it had, it keeps.
Is a heavier object always harder to spin up?
Not necessarily. A heavy compact object can have a smaller \( I \) than a light ring. Mass distribution can outvote total mass.
Why do I need two equations for a pulley problem?
Because two different things are happening: a block translating and a pulley rotating. Each obeys its own law, and \( a = r\alpha \) ties them together.
What about internal torques inside an object?
They cancel in equal-and-opposite pairs, so they never change the spin. Only external torques matter, exactly like external forces in \( F = ma \).
How do I answer "what if" questions without numbers?
Point at the equation. Say which quantity changed, say whether it's on the top or bottom of the fraction, and state the result. That's a complete argument.

5.6 Newton's Second Law in Rotational Form

Topic 5.6 · cheatsheet

5.6 on one page.

Formulas

Everything, one wall

The whole unit in nine boxes.

5.1 · spin rate

\[ \omega_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t} \]

radians per second

5.1 · spin-up rate

\[ \alpha_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta\omega}{\Delta t} \]

rad/s each second

5.1 · the big three

\[ \omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t \]

also \( \theta = \theta_0 + \omega_0t + \tfrac12\alpha t^2 \) and \( \omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\Delta\theta \)

5.2 · the bridges

\[ v = r\omega \]

also \( \Delta s = r\Delta\theta \) and \( a_T = r\alpha \)

5.2 · toward the axis

\[ a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} = r\omega^2 \]

survives constant spin

5.3 · torque

\[ \tau = rF\sin\theta \]

lever arm \( = r\sin\theta \), units N·m

5.4 · rotational inertia

\[ I = \sum m_ir_i^2 \]

units kg·m²

5.4 · shifted axis

\[ I' = I_{\text{cm}} + Md^2 \]

always bigger than \( I_{\text{cm}} \)

5.5 & 5.6 · the laws

\[ \sum\tau = I\alpha \]

zero net torque → constant \( \omega \)

Formulas

The habit

Use the same five steps on every rotation problem.

1

Mark the axis

Every \( r \), every \( I \), every torque is measured from it. Nothing means anything until it's drawn.

2

Pick a positive way

Counterclockwise is the usual choice. Write it on the page so your signs stay honest.

3

Convert units

Degrees → radians. Diameters → radii. Grams → kilograms. Do it before any arithmetic.

4

Choose your law

Nothing changing? \( \sum\tau = 0 \). Spinning up? \( \tau = I\alpha \). Just describing? The big three.

5

Sanity-check

Turn radians into revolutions. Ask if the size feels human. A bike wheel at 600 rad/s is a red flag.

Steps 1 and 3 catch most lost marks. They take about ten seconds and they're the cheapest points in the unit.

Practice

Quick check · 1 / 14

Question

Exam

Don't lose these marks

The mistakes that eat points.

  • 1
    Degrees left in a formula. Convert to radians first. This one silently ruins whole problems.
  • 2
    Dropping the \( \sin\theta \) in torque. Your answer comes out too big and looks plausible. Sketch \( F \) and \( r \) together.
  • 3
    Forgetting to square \( r \) in \( I \). \( mr \) is not a thing. It's \( mr^2 \).
  • 4
    Assuming the two equilibria go together. They're separate conditions. Say which one you mean.
  • 5
    Skipping \( a = r\alpha \) in pulley and rolling problems. Without it you have more unknowns than equations.
  • 6
    Assuming equal tensions on a pulley that has rotational inertia. If they gave you \( I \), they differ.

Free-response gold

When asked "how does X change if Y doubles," don't reach for the calculator. Write the equation, name what's held constant, then say what happens. Three sentences, full marks.

rad, not degrees keep the sine square the r which equilibrium? a = rα T₁ ≠ T₂

Unit 5 is worth about 10–15% of the exam, and torque is the most-missed topic in it. The marks are sitting right there.

Finish

That's the unit

You can read a spin now.

Angles in radians. Multiply by \( r \) to get real speeds. Torque is a twist that needs distance and the right angle. Rotational inertia cares where the mass sits. Balanced twists mean steady spin; leftover twist means \( \alpha = \tau/I \).
